name: Gated batch action
problem: On a rhythm — twice a week, month-end — someone assembles the records that are ready, builds an action for each (an invoice, a payment, a filing), and pushes it into an external system by hand. The rhythm is sacred, the assembly is mechanical, and a fraction of the items always needs judgment.
signals: The work happens on named days and the team has a name for the ritual — 'the sweep', 'the run', 'batch day'.
Eligibility is described as a checklist: delivered AND documented AND not on hold.
A spreadsheet is exported from one system and rekeyed into another, twice a week, by the same person.
Some items are 'always done by hand' and everyone knows which ones without being able to state the rule.
not_for: Event-driven actions, where each record should fire the moment it becomes eligible. That is a different trigger discipline with different failure modes — do not batch what wants to stream.
Actions that cannot be made idempotent or verified afterwards. If you cannot tell whether an action already happened, batching multiplies the damage of every crash.
Eligibility that genuinely cannot be stated as a rule. Automate the assembly and keep the decision human — otherwise you encode one person's folklore as policy.

steps: Select eligible records using an explicit, recorded predicate — never a person's recollection of one.
Resolve cross-system identity through a maintained mapping.
Build each action's payload from the system of record.
Apply the gate: items past the threshold become drafts for a named approver instead of executing.
Execute per item, idempotently, never partially.
Write each result to the flow's own ledger.
Publish a run summary: done, skipped, and — per skip — exactly why, in words the operator can act on.
base_shape.state: Which records were acted on, with the external system's id for each action — the idempotency ledger. Plus the identity mapping, which is data, not code, because it changes on the client's schedule rather than yours.
commitments: Fail closed, per item. An item that errors is skipped whole and reported; it is never half-acted.
Skips are self-healing: the next run picks up anything whose cause was fixed, with no replay ceremony.
The run summary is the product the operator sees. If it does not say why each skip happened in actionable words, the flow is not done.
The gate is a promise to a person, not a performance tolerance. It is removed by that person's word only.

variation_points.question: Run on the client's existing rhythm, or on the technically optimal one?

options.when: The rhythm is load-bearing — other processes, and other people, key off it.
options.consequence: Adoption is instant and the mental model transfers; the rhythm's constraints become yours.

options.when: The ritual was itself a workaround for manual cost, and nothing downstream depends on its timing.
options.consequence: Better latency; every downstream process that quietly keyed off the rhythm must be found first, and they announce themselves by breaking.

variation_points.default_because: The ritual encodes dependencies nobody can enumerate on day one. Ship on their rhythm, then earn the right to change it with evidence from the run summaries.

variation_points.question: Where does human judgment sit relative to execution?

options.when: Stakes are money or customer-visible, or the project was approved on the condition of human review.
options.consequence: Adds a human latency step on gated items; builds the trust the whole project runs on.

options.when: Actions are reversible and volume makes pre-approval impractical.
options.consequence: Full speed; errors reach the outside world before a human sees them, so the undo path must be real.

options.when: Stakes are low and every action is trivially reversible.
options.consequence: Fastest; removes the trust-building surface. Confirm nobody's approval of the project was conditioned on a gate before choosing this.

variation_points.default_because: The gate is usually the political condition the project was approved under. Treat it as a constraint with a named source, record it in the manifest, and no successor will optimize it away by accident.

variation_points.question: Where does the cross-system identity mapping live?

options.when: The mapping changes rarely and an engineer is on retainer to change it.
options.consequence: Every change is a deploy. Fine until the retainer shrinks — then it is a bottleneck with a billing rate.

options.when: The mapping changes whenever the client's business grows.
options.consequence: About two extra days to build, plus validation so a bad row cannot break a run. Removes the engineer from routine change.

variation_points.default_because: 'Nearly static' mappings are not. The reference deployment's mapping changed four times in five months, each change needing an engineer and a deploy — that recorded debt entry is what inverted this default.

variation_points.question: How is double-execution prevented?

options.when: The external system accepts a client-supplied reference and rejects duplicates.
options.consequence: Replays are free; the external system is the ledger of record for what happened.

options.when: The external system offers no idempotency support.
options.consequence: Check-then-act against your own ledger, and reconcile ledger against external system on startup — the crash window between act and record is where doubles are born.

variation_points.default_because: Use the external system's idempotency whenever it exists; your own ledger then becomes a cross-check instead of a single point of truth.

glue_checklist.question: State the eligibility predicate — then reconcile it against historical data before writing code.
glue_checklist.why_it_matters: Ask three people and you get three predicates; the data usually contradicts all of them somewhere. Automating an ambiguous rule produces confidently wrong actions at scale. Carve the ambiguous class out instead — the reference manifest's split-loads decision shows the shape of that call.

glue_checklist.question: Whose approval was this project conditioned on, and what exactly did they ask to keep?
glue_checklist.why_it_matters: The gate threshold is usually a relationship term, not an engineering parameter. Knowing its owner and its reason is the difference between a config value and a betrayal.
glue_checklist.recorded_in: constraints[] (kind: political) with a named source

glue_checklist.question: What are the blackout windows?
glue_checklist.why_it_matters: A batch action running during the client's live window turns a bug into an incident with an audience.
glue_checklist.recorded_in: constraints[] (kind: operational) and the runbook deploy procedure

glue_checklist.question: Who reconciles the skip list, and on what rhythm?
glue_checklist.why_it_matters: Skips self-heal only if someone fixes their causes. An unreconciled skip list grows silently until a customer calls asking where their invoice is.

glue_checklist.question: Can the action be undone, and by whom?
glue_checklist.why_it_matters: Rolling back code does not roll back issued invoices or sent payments. Know the undo path and its owner before the first run, not during the first incident.

human_roles.does: Reviews and releases gated drafts. Politically load-bearing: this role is often the condition the project exists under.
human_roles.cadence: Each run day; minutes, unless a draft is genuinely contentious — which is the role working as designed.
transition_walkthrough_must_cover: What the machine already verified, so review effort goes to judgment rather than re-checking arithmetic.
What releasing a draft actually triggers downstream, in the client's terms.
The escalation path when a draft looks wrong — and that rejecting and telling the steward is always a safe move.

human_roles.does: Owns the skip list from each run summary; fixes causes or routes them to whoever can.
human_roles.cadence: Every run day, immediately after the summary lands.
transition_walkthrough_must_cover: Reading the run summary: each skip reason and its standard fix.
Which skip classes self-heal on the next run versus which need a human first.
The known_failures table in the runbook — most skips are already in it.

human_roles.does: Owns the eligibility predicate, the mapping validation, and the idempotency ledger.
human_roles.cadence: On change; plus a monthly reconciliation of ledger against the external system.
transition_walkthrough_must_cover: The eligibility predicate and the historical evidence it was reconciled against.
The idempotency mechanism, including the crash-window reconciliation on startup.
Why the gate exists, who owns it, and why it is not yours to remove.

failure_design.failure: The run crashes midway through the batch.
failure_design.response: Per-item commits against the ledger; on restart, the ledger — not memory — says what remains. The unit of failure is the item, never the run.

failure_design.failure: The same item is acted on twice, via a crash between act and record.
failure_design.response: A client-supplied idempotency key where the external system honors one; otherwise reconcile ledger against the external system before each run's selection.

failure_design.failure: Mapping drift: newly onboarded records skip with 'not mapped'.
failure_design.response: Skip loudly with the exact missing key in the run summary, and make the fix a data edit rather than a deploy.

failure_design.failure: The eligibility predicate silently drifts from reality because an upstream process changed.
failure_design.response: Track the eligible-count trend across runs. A step change in either direction is an upstream change announcement nobody sent you.

failure_design.failure: The approver is on leave; drafts pile up and the rhythm slips.
failure_design.response: A named delegate with an explicit approval ceiling, recorded in the space definition — and drafts that age visibly in every run summary.

manifest_bindings.systems: The system of record being selected from, the external system being acted on, and wherever the identity mapping lives — each with access, gotchas, and last_verified.
manifest_bindings.entities: The record being acted on and the party it is issued to, with the identifier caveats that make the cross-system mapping necessary in the first place.

decisions_expected.tension: What people say the rule is versus what historical data shows it was — record the reconciliation, and what was carved out as ambiguous.
Throughput versus the trust condition the project was approved under.
The client's ritual versus technically optimal timing.

constraints_expected: The approval condition, as a political constraint with a named source.
Blackout windows around the client's live operations.

metrics.metric: Cycle time from eligible to acted
Percent of items skipped per run
metrics.note: Spikes are upstream news, not flow failures — read them that way first.

metrics.metric: Manually handled items as percent of volume
metrics.note: Should fall slowly as carve-outs get resolved into rules. Falling fast usually means someone stopped checking.

metrics.metric: Rhythm adherence (runs completed on their scheduled day)

deviations: Identity mapping still lives in the repo — recorded there as debt with a cost_to_fix, and the experience that flipped this pattern's default to editable-table.
Split loads carved out of automation entirely rather than parameterized, because three people described the allocation rule three different ways (see decision split-loads-manual).

maturity.evidence: One shipped deployment (Meridian invoice issuance). The editable-table default is a lesson from that deployment's recorded debt rather than something it shipped — flagged so users know which parts are proven and which are corrected hindsight.
